column1: In account management, what is the fundamental conceptual inversion compared to sales regarding how the customer is treated?
column2: Sales treats the customer as a destination (end of the transaction); account management treats the customer as a point of departure (start of a time-dimensioned relationship).

column1: What is the typical CAC payback period range for a mid-market SaaS business, and why does this matter architecturally?
column2: 18 to 30 months. It means the initial sale doesn't cover acquisition cost, so the entire commercial thesis depends on retention and expansion over time — making lifecycle management an architectural necessity, not an optional function.

column1: What is the first invariant of account lifecycle management regarding deteriorating vs. healthy relationships?
column2: The cost to rescue a deteriorating relationship always exceeds the cost to maintain a healthy one — typically by 4 to 6 times the effort (executive re-engagement, concessions, custom roadmaps vs. a thoughtful QBR).

column1: What is the second invariant linking expansion and retention in account management?
column2: Expansion and retention are not independent variables — both depend on the same underlying conditions: realized value, organizational adoption, and trust in the vendor's execution.

column1: What invariant must segment boundaries satisfy in a customer segmentation model?
column2: Segment boundaries must correlate with both the cost-to-serve and the revenue ceiling of the account — ensuring coverage models (e.g., high-touch CSM vs. self-serve) are economically defensible.

column1: Calculate the coverage ratio for a CSM with fully-loaded cost of $120,000 managing 20 enterprise accounts at $200,000 ACV each. Is this ratio economically viable?
column2: Book of business = 20 × $200,000 = $4,000,000. Coverage ratio = $4,000,000 / $120,000 = 33x. Yes, this is economically viable for strategic high-touch coverage.

column1: Why is segment stability (not reclassifying customers every quarter) considered an invariant in segmentation design?
column2: Because sales, marketing, support, and product all build operational motions around segment definitions; frequent reclassification introduces coordination costs that negate the analytical benefits of segmentation.

column1: What are the three interconnected mechanisms through which enterprise customer value accrues in strategic account management?
column2: 1) Consumption expansion (deeper usage of existing capabilities), 2) Portfolio expansion (cross-sell of additional products/modules), 3) Strategic partnership elevation (deep integration creating switching costs and executive dependency).

column1: What organizational constraint limits how aggressively a strategic account manager can pursue simultaneous expansion vectors?
column2: Enterprise organizations have finite attention bandwidth, political capital reserves, and change management capacity — exceeding this absorption capacity triggers 'immune responses' like procurement commoditization or champion burnout.

column1: What is the first invariant of enterprise account architecture regarding organizational complexity and company size?
column2: Organizational complexity scales non-linearly with company size — large enterprises involve many veto-holding constituencies (procurement, legal, infosec, architecture boards) none of which individually guarantees deal closure.

column1: What does it mean that enterprise accounts 'generate revenue through expansion, not replacement,' and what NRR figure typically reflects this?
column2: The initial contract is a beachhead; compounding revenue comes from land-and-expand motion (new business units, modules, services). Enterprise portfolios routinely show Net Revenue Retention (NRR) exceeding 120%.

column1: In the Customer Health Score (CHS) model, what is the core theoretical premise linking leading indicators to churn?
column2: Silent attrition is preceded by measurable decay in leading indicators — primarily product stickiness (usage) and technical friction (support signals) — such that the health score crosses a red-zone threshold before any verbal churn signal from the client.
